lessons.title: 0/1 Knapsack Pattern
lessons.objective: Implement 0/1 knapsack using 2D DP and the space-optimised 1D version with right-to-left iteration, and understand why each item can be used at most once.
concepts: 0/1 knapsack: each item used at most once (0 or 1 times)
State: dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w
Transition: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i]] + val[i])
Include vs exclude decision at every item
O(n*W) time and space for 2D version
1D space optimisation: iterate weights RIGHT TO LEFT
Why right-to-left: prevents using the same item twice
Unbounded knapsack: iterate left to right (reuse allowed)
lessons.explanation: The 0/1 knapsack problem: given n items each with a weight and value, and a knapsack with capacity W, maximise the total value without exceeding W, using each item at most once. The 2D DP: dp[i][w] = maximum value achievable using the first i items with weight capacity w. Transition: for item i with weight wt and value val, either exclude it (dp[i-1][w]) or include it if wt <= w (dp[i-1][w-wt] + val). dp[i][w] = max of these two. The key distinction from unbounded knapsack: dp[i-1][w-wt] (not dp[i][w-wt]) is used because item i can only be used once. Using dp[i] on the right side would allow reusing the same item. Space optimisation: collapse to 1D by iterating weights from right to left. The right-to-left order ensures that when dp[w-wt] is read, it still reflects the state before item i was considered (the i-1 row). Left-to-right would allow item i to be counted multiple times, turning it into unbounded knapsack.
lessons.analogy: 0/1 knapsack is a packing problem where each item exists as a single physical object: you either pack it or leave it. To decide whether to include a given item, you compare: the best packing without this item (dp[i-1][w]) versus the best packing using this item (dp[i-1][w-wt]+val). The right-to-left iteration in the 1D version is like packing from the largest capacity bag to the smallest: when you check whether item i fits in a bag of size w, you consult the bag of size w-wt from BEFORE you started considering item i today, not after.

code_example.explanation: The right-to-left vs left-to-right iteration is the single most important detail in knapsack DP. Right-to-left: each item used at most once (0/1 knapsack). Left-to-right: each item used any number of times (unbounded knapsack, same as Coin Change). The loop direction determines which version of the problem you are solving.

common_mistakes: Iterating weights left-to-right in 0/1 knapsack — this allows an item to be counted multiple times within the same pass; always iterate right-to-left for 0/1 and left-to-right for unbounded

Using dp[i][w-wt] instead of dp[i-1][w-wt] in the 2D version — dp[i][w-wt] would allow item i to be included multiple times in the same row (unbounded); the i-1 row ensures each item is used at most once
Starting the inner loop at w=0 instead of w=wt in the 1D version — for w < wt the item cannot fit and dp[w] should not change; the loop should start at w=capacity and go down to w=wt (inclusive)
lessons.interview_relevance: 0/1 knapsack is the foundational pattern for Target Sum, Partition Equal Subset Sum, and Ones and Zeros in NeetCode 150. Interviewers ask 'why right-to-left?' after a candidate produces the 1D version. The answer — 'to ensure dp[w-wt] reflects the state before item i was considered, preventing reuse of the same item' — demonstrates genuine DP understanding.

flashcards.front: 0/1 Knapsack: 2D recurrence?
flashcards.back: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i-1]] + val[i-1]) if wt[i-1] ≤ w, else dp[i-1][w]. First i items, capacity w. Note dp[i-1] (not dp[i]) on the include branch — ensures each item used at most once.

flashcards.front: 0/1 Knapsack 1D: why iterate RIGHT TO LEFT?
flashcards.back: Right-to-left ensures dp[w-wt] reads the value from BEFORE item i was considered (same as dp[i-1][w-wt] in 2D). Left-to-right would let item i update dp[wt], then dp[2wt] reads that updated value — effectively using item i twice.

flashcards.front: 0/1 vs Unbounded Knapsack: the single difference?
flashcards.back: 0/1 (each item once): inner weight loop goes RIGHT TO LEFT (high → low). Unbounded (reuse allowed): inner loop goes LEFT TO RIGHT (low → high). SAME recurrence dp[w]=max(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val), only the loop direction differs.

flashcards.front: 0/1 Knapsack 1D space: what is the dp array size?
flashcards.back: dp of size capacity+1. dp[w] = best value achievable with weight capacity exactly w (or at most w depending on initialisation). Initialise all to 0 for maximisation.

flashcards.front: Three variants of knapsack DP?
flashcards.back: MAX VALUE: dp[w]=max(dp[w], dp[w-wt]+val). COUNT WAYS: dp[w]+=dp[w-wt]. BOOLEAN: dp[w]|=dp[w-wt]. All use RIGHT-TO-LEFT for 0/1 (each item once) and LEFT-TO-RIGHT for unbounded (reuse). Same pattern, different operation.

flashcards.front: How to backtrack which items were selected in 0/1 Knapsack?
flashcards.back: Use the 2D table. Start at dp[n][W]. If dp[i][w] > dp[i-1][w]: item i was included. Set w = w - wt[i-1] and move to i-1. If dp[i][w] == dp[i-1][w]: item i was excluded. Move to i-1. Repeat until i=0.

quiz.question: 0/1 Knapsack 1D: weights=[2,3], values=[3,4], capacity=5. After processing item 0 (wt=2,val=3), dp=?
After also processing item 1 (wt=3,val=4) on dp=[0,0,3,3,3,3], what is dp[5]?
quiz.explanation: Right-to-left: w=5: dp[5]=max(3, dp[2]+4)=max(3,3+4)=7. Item 0 (wt=2) + item 1 (wt=3) = capacity 5, value 3+4=7. ✓

quiz.question: In 0/1 knapsack 2D, the include branch uses dp[i-1][w-wt] not dp[i][w-wt]. Why?
options: To handle the base case i=0
dp[i][w-wt] would allow item i to be included multiple times in the same row
dp[i-1] is faster to access
Only dp[i-1] is computed at this point
quiz.explanation: dp[i][w-wt] would reference the current row where item i might already be included. Using dp[i-1][w-wt] explicitly restricts to 'before item i was considered', enforcing the at-most-once constraint.

quiz.question: Left-to-right 0/1 knapsack inner loop: what bug does this introduce?
options: Off-by-one in the dp array
Item i can be counted multiple times (becomes unbounded knapsack)
dp[0] becomes non-zero
The capacity constraint is violated
quiz.explanation: Left-to-right: dp[wt] is updated first using dp[0] (includes item i once). Then dp[2wt] is updated using the newly updated dp[wt] — item i is counted again. This is unbounded knapsack, not 0/1.

theory_mcq.question: In the 1D space-optimised knapsack, why must weights be iterated RIGHT TO LEFT rather than left to right?
options: Right-to-left is required for JavaScript array compatibility

LEFT-TO-RIGHT would allow the same item to be counted multiple times (unbounded knapsack): dp[wt] is updated first, then dp[2*wt] sees the ALREADY-UPDATED dp[wt] and adds the item again; RIGHT-TO-LEFT ensures dp[w-wt] is still from BEFORE the current item was considered — the old row value — so each item contributes at most once per pass; this is the exact distinction between 0/1 (right-to-left) and unbounded (left-to-right) knapsack
Left-to-right causes array index out of bounds
Both directions give identical results; the direction is a stylistic choice
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact comment: 'CRITICAL: iterate RIGHT TO LEFT. This ensures dp[w-wt] is from BEFORE item i was considered' and 'If we iterated LEFT TO RIGHT: dp[wt] updated first → includes item i once; dp[2wt] updated next → sees dp[wt] already updated → includes item i TWICE. That would be unbounded knapsack, not 0/1'.

theory_mcq.question: In the 2D knapsack, `dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]` is set BEFORE checking the include case. What does this initialisation represent?
options: It is a placeholder that gets overwritten in every case

It represents the EXCLUDE ITEM i decision: `dp[i-1][w]` is the best value achievable using only the FIRST i-1 items with capacity w; setting this as the default means 'not taking item i is always a valid option'; the include case then checks whether taking item i (`dp[i-1][w-wt]+val`) improves on this baseline; the max of exclude and include gives the optimal 0/1 decision
It copies the previous row's capacity; it has no semantic meaning
It initialises dp[i][w] to 0 before the comparison
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Include vs exclude decision at every item' and the code: `dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]; // exclude item i` — the exclude decision is always valid (skip item i); the include decision is conditionally valid (only if wt<=w); the recurrence takes the maximum of the two valid options.

logic_mcq.question: For knapsack with weights=[2,3,4,5], values=[3,4,5,6], capacity=8, the answer is 10. Which items are selected and what is their combined weight?
options: Items 0 and 2 (wt=2+4=6, val=3+5=8); answer=8

Items 1 and 3 (wt=3+5=8, val=4+6=10); combined weight exactly equals capacity=8; this is optimal because no combination achieves higher value within capacity — confirmed by direct execution of both 2D and 1D versions returning 10
Items 0, 1, and 2 (wt=2+3+4=9>8); infeasible
Item 3 alone (wt=5, val=6); answer=6
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: knapsack returns 10; verifying item1(wt=3,val=4)+item3(wt=5,val=6)=wt8,val10 exactly meets capacity=8; other combinations: item0+item2=wt6,val8; item0+item3=wt7,val9; item1+item2=wt7,val9; item2+item3=wt9>8 infeasible; item1+item3=wt8,val10 is optimal.

logic_mcq.question: What is the difference between 0/1 knapsack (right-to-left) and UNBOUNDED knapsack (left-to-right) in terms of WHAT THEY COMPUTE?
options: Both compute the same result; only the performance differs

0/1 KNAPSACK: each item can be selected AT MOST ONCE — you're deciding to include or exclude each item; RIGHT-TO-LEFT iteration ensures each item's effect is seen only once per pass; UNBOUNDED KNAPSACK: each item can be used ANY NUMBER OF TIMES — you can keep adding the same coin/item; LEFT-TO-RIGHT iteration allows an item's updated value to propagate forward and be reused in the same pass; Coin Change II is unbounded (coins reusable), while Partition Subset Sum is 0/1 (each number used once)
Unbounded is strictly better than 0/1; always use left-to-right
0/1 only works for binary items; unbounded only works for coins
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit comparison: 'Unbounded knapsack: iterate left to right (reuse allowed)' vs '0/1 knapsack: iterate right to left (each item once)' — the iteration direction is the single code change that switches between these two fundamental variants; the lesson's comment traces exactly how left-to-right causes double-counting.

syntax_mcq.question: In `knapsack01_1D`, the inner loop starts at `w = capacity` and decrements to `w = wt` (stops at wt, not 0). Why stop at `wt` rather than at 0?
options: Stopping at 0 would cause negative array indexing

When `w < wt`, the item CANNOT FIT into a bag of capacity w — `w - wt` would be negative, making `dp[w-wt]` an invalid access; since items with weight > remaining capacity can never be included, the loop stops at `wt` (the minimum capacity where this item fits); positions 0 to wt-1 are left unchanged because they cannot benefit from including this item
The loop stops at wt for performance only; extending to 0 gives the same result
Stopping at wt prevents overflow when computing dp[w-wt]
syntax_mcq.explanation: The condition `for (let w = capacity; w >= wt; w--)` is equivalent to the 2D version's `if (wt <= w)` guard — positions w < wt cannot accommodate the item (w-wt < 0), so they're correctly skipped; looping from capacity down to wt covers exactly the positions where the item fits.

lessons.title: Target Sum
lessons.objective: Solve Target Sum by reducing it to a 0/1 knapsack subset sum problem using the mathematical reduction from +/- assignments to subset sums.
concepts: Target Sum: assign + or - to each number to reach target
Naive: DFS with +/- at each position O(2^n)
Mathematical reduction: partition numbers into P (plus) and N (minus)
P - N = target, P + N = sum -> P = (sum + target) / 2
Reduced problem: count subsets summing to (sum+target)/2
0/1 knapsack count variant: dp[j] += dp[j - num]
Validity check: (sum+target) must be even and non-negative
O(n * sum) time, O(sum) space
lessons.explanation: Target Sum (#494) assigns + or - to each number to reach a target. The naive DFS explores 2^n assignments. The key mathematical insight: partition numbers into two groups P (assigned +) and N (assigned -). Then P - N = target and P + N = total_sum. Adding these: 2P = target + sum, so P = (target + sum) / 2. Now the problem becomes: how many ways to choose a subset of numbers summing to P? This is the subset sum count problem, a 0/1 knapsack variant. The DP: dp[j] = number of subsets summing to j. Base case: dp[0] = 1 (one way to make sum 0: empty subset). Transition: for each number, update dp right-to-left (0/1): dp[j] += dp[j - num]. Validity check: (target + sum) must be even (otherwise P is not an integer) and non-negative (target > sum is impossible). This reduction is a classic DP trick: transform the original problem into an equivalent one with a known DP pattern.
lessons.analogy: Target Sum reduction is like splitting a group of people into two teams where one team's total minus the other's equals a target score. Instead of trying every possible team assignment, you realise the winning team must have a specific total score determined by the target and the total of everyone. Now the problem is simply: how many ways can you form the winning team with that exact score? This is a well-known problem (subset sum) with a known efficient solution.

code_example.explanation: The reduction P = (sum + target) / 2 works because: every number is in exactly one of two groups (plus or minus). The plus group sums to P, the minus group sums to N = sum - P. P - N = P - (sum - P) = 2P - sum = target, which gives P = (sum + target) / 2. When nums contains zeros, they can be in either group without affecting sums — dp[0] accumulates ways correctly since dp[j-0] = dp[j].

common_mistakes: Forgetting to check that (sum + target) is even — if it is odd, P would be a non-integer and there are zero valid assignments; always validate parity before building the DP
Not checking abs(target) <= sum — if |target| > sum, it is impossible to reach the target even by making all numbers positive or all negative; return 0 immediately
Iterating left-to-right instead of right-to-left in the knapsack loop — target sum uses 0/1 knapsack (each number used once), which requires right-to-left iteration
lessons.interview_relevance: Target Sum (#494) is NeetCode 150 and a favourite meta-interview problem because it requires a non-obvious mathematical reduction before any DP. Interviewers specifically test whether candidates know to look for a reduction before coding. The ability to state 'I can reduce this to counting subsets summing to (sum+target)/2' within 2 minutes of reading the problem is a strong signal.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement findTargetSumWays and verify it returns 5 for ([1,1,1,1,1], 3). Derive the mathematical reduction yourself: start from P - N = target and P + N = sum and show the algebraic steps to P = (sum + target) / 2. Then solve Ones and Zeros (LeetCode #474): given strings of 0s and 1s and capacity m zeros and n ones, find the maximum number of strings you can pick. This is a 2D 0/1 knapsack where the capacity is a pair (m, n).

flashcards.front: Target Sum mathematical reduction?
flashcards.back: Let P = set assigned '+', N = set assigned '-'. P - N = target, P + N = total. Adding: 2P = target + total → P = (target + total) / 2. Problem reduces to: count subsets summing to P.

flashcards.front: Target Sum validity checks?
flashcards.back: 1) (target + total) must be EVEN — else P is not an integer, return 0. 2) abs(target) ≤ total — else impossible even with all signs positive/negative, return 0.

flashcards.front: Target Sum DP: what does dp[j] represent?
flashcards.back: Number of subsets of nums that sum to exactly j. This is the COUNT variant of 0/1 knapsack: dp[j] += dp[j-num] (not max, not boolean — += for counting).

flashcards.front: Target Sum DP base case?
flashcards.back: dp[0] = 1. There is exactly ONE subset summing to 0: the empty subset. All other dp[j] start at 0.

flashcards.front: Target Sum: what changes if nums contains zeros?
flashcards.back: Each 0 can be in either the + or - group without affecting sums. dp[j-0] = dp[j], so dp[j] += dp[j] → doubles the count for each 0. The DP handles this correctly automatically since j≥0 and dp[j]+=dp[j-0]=dp[j] doubles dp[j].

flashcards.front: Target Sum: DFS vs DP — complexity comparison?
flashcards.back: DFS: O(2^n) — tries all +/- assignments. DP after reduction: O(n × P) where P=(sum+target)/2 ≤ sum. For n=20, sum=1000: DFS ≈ 1M calls, DP ≈ 20,000 operations. DP is dramatically faster.

Either direction works for counting

theory_mcq.question: What is the MATHEMATICAL REDUCTION that transforms Target Sum from a +/- assignment problem into a 0/1 knapsack subset sum problem?
options: Sort the array and greedily assign signs based on position

Let P = set of numbers with '+' and N = set with '-'; then P - N = target AND P + N = sum; solving: P = (sum + target) / 2; therefore, counting assignments that achieve `target` is equivalent to counting SUBSETS THAT SUM TO (sum+target)/2; this converts the exponential DFS (2^n) to O(n*sum) knapsack counting; validity requires (sum+target) to be even and non-negative
The reduction only works when all numbers are equal
Target Sum is always solved by DFS; no knapsack reduction exists
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact derivation: 'P - N = target, P + N = sum → P = (sum + target) / 2' — this algebraic manipulation converts the two-constraint problem (sum of all + sum of minuses = target) into a single-constraint counting problem (count subsets summing to a fixed target), enabling the efficient O(n*sum) knapsack approach.

theory_mcq.question: What are the TWO VALIDITY CHECKS needed before proceeding with the knapsack reduction?
options: Check that target > 0 and all numbers are positive

(1) `(sum + target) % 2 !== 0`: if sum+target is odd, P=(sum+target)/2 is not an integer — no valid partition exists, return 0; (2) `Math.abs(target) > sum`: if |target| exceeds the total sum, even assigning all signs to one side can't reach target — return 0; both checks prevent computing a negative or non-integer subsetTarget which would produce meaningless DP results
Check that the array is sorted and has no duplicates
Check that target is less than max element
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact code: 'if ((sum + target) % 2 !== 0) return 0; // (sum+target) must be even' and 'if (Math.abs(target) > sum) return 0; // target unreachable' — these guard against mathematically impossible cases before the DP allocation, preventing integer/index errors.

logic_mcq.question: For `findTargetSumWays([1,1,1,1,1], target=3)`: what is the `subsetTarget` computed by the reduction, and why is the answer C(5,4)=5?
options: subsetTarget=3; answer=5 because there are 5 ways to assign 3 pluses

sum=5, subsetTarget=(5+3)/2=4; we count subsets of five 1s that sum to 4; any 4 of the 5 ones sum to 4; there are C(5,4)=5 ways to choose 4 items from 5; the 5th item gets assigned '-' in each case; confirmed by direct execution returning 5
subsetTarget=4; answer=5 by coincidence with the target value
subsetTarget=4; answer is computed by the naive DFS as C(5,2)=10
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace: 'nums=[1,1,1,1,1], target=3: sum=5, P=(5+3)/2=4. Find: how many subsets of [1,1,1,1,1] sum to 4? Answer: C(5,4) = 5 (choose any 4 of the 5 ones)' — confirmed by direct execution returning 5.

logic_mcq.question: In `findTargetSumWays`, `dp[j] += dp[j - num]` (right-to-left) counts COMBINATIONS. What would happen if this loop ran LEFT-TO-RIGHT?
options: Left-to-right would give the same result since addition is commutative

Left-to-right would count PERMUTATIONS (ordered sequences), not combinations: once dp[num] is updated to include a sequence ending with this number, dp[2*num] would see the updated dp[num] and count a sequence that uses this number TWICE — equivalent to the Coin Change II permutation bug from Module 2; for example, with nums=[1,1] and target=0, the count would be inflated beyond the correct value
Left-to-right would always return 0
Left-to-right would be more efficient and still correct
logic_mcq.explanation: The same right-to-left / left-to-right distinction as 0/1 vs unbounded knapsack: right-to-left ensures each number is used at most once per assignment (0/1 semantics); left-to-right would let each number's contribution propagate forward and be counted multiple times (unbounded semantics), inflating the count beyond the correct answer.

syntax_mcq.question: In `findTargetSumWays`, `dp[0] = 1` initialises with 'one way to make sum 0: empty subset'. Why is this the correct base case for a COUNTING knapsack?
options: dp[0]=1 is wrong; it should be 0 since no items have been selected

For COUNTING problems, dp[j] = number of subsets summing to j; the empty subset is a valid subset and it sums to 0 — so there is exactly 1 way to achieve sum 0 (select nothing); dp[0]=1 seeds all subsequent transitions: when `dp[j] += dp[j-num]`, if j==num, dp[num] += dp[0] = 1, correctly counting the subset {num} as one way to reach sum num; dp[0]=0 would incorrectly prevent any single-element subsets from being counted
dp[0]=1 is the same as dp[0]=true used in boolean knapsack
The base case should be dp[0]=0 for counting and dp[0]=1 only for max-value problems
syntax_mcq.explanation: The counting base case dp[0]=1 is universal for subset-count DP: 'there is exactly 1 way to form sum 0 — the empty selection'; this is the counting analog of dp[0]=true in boolean knapsack (exists a subset summing to 0) and dp[0]=0 in min-coins (0 coins needed for amount 0); getting the base case right is what makes the entire recurrence produce correct counts.

lessons.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
lessons.objective: Solve Partition Equal Subset Sum as a boolean 0/1 knapsack, determining whether a subset summing to exactly sum/2 exists.
concepts: Partition into two equal subsets: each half sums to total/2
Necessary condition: total sum must be even
Reduction: can any subset sum to total/2? (boolean 0/1 knapsack)
dp[j] = true if subset summing to j is achievable
Transition: dp[j] |= dp[j - num] (right-to-left)
Early termination: return true as soon as dp[total/2] becomes true
O(n * sum/2) time, O(sum/2) space
Boolean knapsack vs count knapsack vs max-value knapsack
lessons.explanation: Partition Equal Subset Sum (#416) asks whether a set of integers can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sums. For this to be possible, the total sum must be even (otherwise equal halves are impossible). If even, check whether any subset sums to total/2. If yes, the remaining elements form the other half automatically. The DP is a boolean 0/1 knapsack: dp[j] = true if a subset summing to exactly j is achievable using some elements. Base case: dp[0] = true (empty subset sums to 0). Transition: for each number, iterate right-to-left. For each capacity j from target down to num: dp[j] |= dp[j - num]. This means: if we could previously achieve sum j-num, we can now achieve sum j by including this number. The answer is dp[target]. Early termination optimisation: if dp[target] becomes true during any inner loop iteration, return true immediately.
lessons.analogy: Partition Equal Subset Sum is like splitting a group of objects into two equal-weight groups using a balance scale. You check the total weight first: if it is odd, immediately impossible. If even, the question is: can I form a group that weighs exactly half the total? You try to pack a bag of exactly half-total capacity. If you succeed, the remaining items automatically form the other half.

code_example.explanation: The early termination if (dp[target]) return true is an important optimisation. Once the target subset sum is found, there is no need to process remaining numbers. In the worst case (no partition exists), all numbers are processed. In the best case (partition found after the first few numbers), significant work is avoided.

common_mistakes: Not checking that the total is even before building the DP table — if total is odd, target would be a non-integer and the dp array would have the wrong size; always check parity first

Iterating left-to-right (unbounded) instead of right-to-left (0/1) — left-to-right would allow using the same number multiple times, which would make [1,2,3] report true for target=4 (using 1 twice) when 1+1+2=4 is not a valid subset
Not initialising dp[0] = true — the base case represents the empty subset (always achievable); without it, no subset can ever be formed because all transitions require a reachable smaller sum

theory_mcq.question: What are the THREE VARIANTS of the 1D knapsack and how does each use `dp[j]`?
options: All three use dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j-num]; only the initialization differs

MAX VALUE: `dp[j] = Math.max(dp[j], dp[j-wt]+val)` — tracks optimal value; COUNT WAYS: `dp[j] += dp[j-num]` — accumulates number of valid selections; BOOLEAN: `dp[j] |= dp[j-num]` or `dp[j] = dp[j] || dp[j-num]` — tracks existence; all three use RIGHT-TO-LEFT for 0/1 (each item once) and LEFT-TO-RIGHT for unbounded (item reusable); the variant is chosen based on what question is being answered
Max-value uses a 2D table; count and boolean can only be 1D
Boolean knapsack uses left-to-right; the other two use right-to-left
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit side-by-side: 'Max value: dp[j]=Math.max(dp[j],dp[j-wt]+val); Count ways: dp[j]+=dp[j-num]; Boolean: dp[j]|=dp[j-num]' — this classification is the core conceptual framework for all knapsack-family problems; recognizing which variant to use is the key skill.

theory_mcq.question: Why can we use EARLY TERMINATION (`if (dp[target]) return true`) inside the outer loop of `canPartition`?
options: Early termination is a bug; we must always process all numbers

Once `dp[target]` becomes true, we have CONFIRMED that a valid subset exists summing to target — the partitioning is possible; processing remaining numbers cannot change a true back to false (boolean OR operation is monotonic: once true, stays true); returning immediately saves unnecessary computation for the remaining numbers; this is a correctness-preserving optimization identical to early termination in string search algorithms
Early termination only works when the array is sorted
dp[target]=true means the algorithm is done; processing more would corrupt the table
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code comment: 'early exit' — the boolean OR knapsack is monotonically increasing: values transition from false to true but never back; once dp[target]=true, the answer is confirmed regardless of remaining elements; this optimization reduces practical runtime significantly for inputs that quickly find a valid partition.

total=22, target=11; after num=1: dp[1]=T → dp=[T,T,F,...F]; after num=5 (right-to-left, j=11..5): dp[6]=dp[6-5=1]=T→T; dp[5]=dp[5-5=0]=T→T; result: dp=[T,T,F,F,F,T,T,F,F,F,F,F]; positions 0,1,5,6 are now reachable — matching the lesson's trace exactly
After num=5: dp=[T,T,F,F,F,T,F,F,F,F,F,F]; only 5 is newly reachable
After num=5: dp=[T,F,F,F,F,T,F,F,F,F,F,F]; 1 was overwritten

logic_mcq.question: Why does `canPartition([1,2,5])` return false despite total=8 and target=4 being integers?
options: It returns true; {1,3} sums to 4 but 3 is not in the array

No subset of {1,2,5} sums to 4: {1}=1, {2}=2, {5}=5>4, {1,2}=3, {1,5}=6>4, {2,5}=7>4, {1,2,5}=8>4; none equals 4; the DP confirms this by finding dp[4]=false after all elements are processed — confirmed by direct execution returning false
The algorithm incorrectly rejects this because 8 is even
canPartition would return true with right-to-left iteration
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: canPartition([1,2,5])=false; checking all 7 non-empty subsets of {1,2,5}: none sums to 4; the DP correctly reflects this — dp[4] remains false because no combination of the available numbers can form exactly 4.

syntax_mcq.question: In `canPartition`, `if (dp[j - num]) dp[j] = true` can be written as `dp[j] = dp[j] || dp[j - num]`. Which form is SAFER and why?
options: Both are identical; there is no safety difference

The `dp[j] = dp[j] || dp[j-num]` form is SAFER because: (1) it handles the case where dp[j] is ALREADY true (keeps it true without the conditional branch); (2) the `||` short-circuits — if dp[j] is already true, dp[j-num] is not even evaluated; (3) it explicitly represents the boolean OR semantics of the knapsack; the `if (dp[j-num]) dp[j]=true` form is also correct but requires reading dp[j]'s current value implicitly
The if-form is safer; the ||= form can corrupt the dp array
dp[j]=true is correct; the || form would sometimes set dp[j] to false
syntax_mcq.explanation: Both forms are semantically equivalent for this problem; `dp[j] = dp[j] || dp[j-num]` is more explicit about the boolean OR semantics and short-circuits when dp[j] is already true (minor optimization); the if-form `if (dp[j-num]) dp[j]=true` never sets dp[j] to false once it's been set, making both forms monotonically correct for the boolean knapsack.

lessons.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
lessons.objective: Solve LIS in O(n²) with standard DP and O(n log n) with patience sorting, and understand the binary search invariant that enables the optimal solution.
concepts: LIS: longest subsequence where each element is strictly greater than the previous
dp[i] = length of LIS ending at index i
O(n^2) transition: for all j<i where nums[j]<nums[i]: dp[i]=max(dp[i],dp[j]+1)
O(n^2) answer: max over all dp[i]
O(n log n) patience sorting: maintain 'piles' with smallest top
tails array invariant: tails[k] = smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length k+1
Binary search: find leftmost position in tails where tails[pos] >= current element
Replace tails[pos] or extend: length of tails is the LIS length
lessons.explanation: Longest Increasing Subsequence (#300) finds the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The O(n²) DP: dp[i] = length of the LIS ending exactly at index i. For each i, look back at all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i] and take the maximum dp[j] + 1. Base case: dp[i] = 1 (every element is a LIS of length 1 by itself). Answer: max over all dp[i]. The O(n log n) approach uses a 'tails' array maintaining a critical invariant: tails[k] is the smallest tail element of all increasing subsequences of length k+1. Process each element: binary search for the leftmost position in tails where tails[pos] >= current element. Replace tails[pos] with the current element (or extend tails if not found). The length of tails at the end is the LIS length. The binary search makes each step O(log n) instead of O(n).
lessons.analogy: O(n log n) LIS is like a card game called Patience. You deal cards one at a time. Each card goes onto the leftmost pile whose top card is >= the current card. If no such pile exists, start a new pile. The goal is to minimise the number of piles. By the mathematical structure of the game, the minimum number of piles always equals the LIS length. Binary search finds the correct pile in O(log n) instead of scanning all piles.

code_example.explanation: tails never stores an actual LIS — it is a structural device. After processing [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18], tails = [2,3,7,18] which is NOT the actual LIS [2,5,7,101] or [2,3,7,101]. The invariant guarantees only that tails.length equals the LIS length. This is a common point of confusion: the tails array tracks the optimal tail values, not the actual subsequence.

common_mistakes: Using <= instead of < in the O(n²) transition condition — LIS requires strictly increasing (nums[j] < nums[i]); using <= would count equal elements as increasing, giving wrong answers for arrays with duplicates

Thinking the tails array is an actual LIS — tails is a structural optimisation tool that only guarantees its length equals the LIS length; reconstructing the actual LIS requires a separate parent array in the O(n²) version

Using the wrong binary search variant in O(n log n) — we need the leftmost position where tails[pos] >= num (lower bound); using upper bound (tails[pos] > num) would allow equal elements and count them as increasing

lessons.title: Edit Distance
lessons.objective: Implement Edit Distance using 2D DP with three operation types, apply the space-optimised single-row version, and connect it to LCS as the same string alignment framework.
concepts: Edit Distance: minimum insertions, deletions, substitutions to transform word1 to word2
dp[i][j] = min edits to transform word1[0..i-1] to word2[0..j-1]
Match: word1[i-1]==word2[j-1] -> dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (free)
Substitute: dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
Delete from word1: dp[i-1][j] + 1
Insert into word1 (= delete from word2): dp[i][j-1] + 1
Base cases: dp[i][0] = i, dp[0][j] = j
O(m*n) time, O(n) space with single-row optimisation
lessons.explanation: Edit Distance (#72) (Levenshtein distance) finds the minimum number of single-character edits (insert, delete, substitute) to transform word1 into word2. The 2D DP: dp[i][j] = minimum edits to transform word1[0..i-1] into word2[0..j-1]. Base cases: dp[0][j] = j (insert j characters into empty string) and dp[i][0] = i (delete all i characters). Transition: if word1[i-1] equals word2[j-1], no edit is needed: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise, take the minimum of three operations: substitute (dp[i-1][j-1] + 1), delete from word1 (dp[i-1][j] + 1), or insert into word1 / delete from word2 (dp[i][j-1] + 1). Space optimisation: dp[i][j] depends only on the current row and the previous row, so two rows suffice. Further: with careful ordering, a single row with one extra variable can store the diagonal. Edit Distance and LCS are in the same family: LCS counts matches, Edit Distance counts the minimum mismatches (edits). Both use the same 2D table structure with the same match/mismatch case split.
lessons.analogy: Edit Distance is like counting the minimum keystrokes to retype a word from memory when you realise you mistyped it. Each keystroke is either a substitution (press the right key instead of the wrong one), a deletion (backspace), or an insertion (add a missing character). The DP table computes this optimally for every prefix pair, building up to the full word transformation.

code_example.explanation: The three operations in the transition correspond to three adjacent cells in the DP table. Substitute: dp[i-1][j-1] (diagonal) — change the current character. Delete from word1: dp[i-1][j] (above) — skip a character in word1. Insert into word1 (equivalently, delete from word2): dp[i][j-1] (left) — skip a character in word2. These three directions in the table directly correspond to the three edit operations.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the base cases dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j — these represent converting to/from an empty string (all deletions or all insertions); missing them leaves the first row and column uninitialised
Using the wrong operation for dp[i][j-1] — this operation is 'skip a character in word2', which corresponds to inserting that character into word1 (or deleting it from word2); the cost is always 1

Confusing Edit Distance with LCS — LCS adds 1 on a match and takes max on mismatch; Edit Distance adds 0 on a match and takes 1+min on mismatch; the table structures are the same but the operations differ
lessons.interview_relevance: Edit Distance (#72) is NeetCode 150 and one of the most prestigious DP problems. It appears at Google, Meta, and Stripe specifically because it tests whether a candidate can define a 2D DP state with multiple transition types. The connection to LCS (same structure, different semantics) demonstrates DP pattern recognition depth.

lessons.title: Burst Balloons — Hard
lessons.objective: Solve Burst Balloons using interval DP by inverting the problem to consider the last balloon burst in each interval rather than the first.
concepts: Burst Balloons: burst balloon i, earn nums[i-1]*nums[i]*nums[i+1]
Naive: try all permutations O(n!) or greedy fails
Key insight: think LAST balloon to burst, not first
Add sentinel 1s at both ends: nums = [1, ...nums, 1]
dp[i][j] = max coins from bursting all balloons strictly between i and j
Transition: for each k in (i,j), k is the LAST balloon burst in interval (i,j)
dp[i][j] = max over k of (nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] + dp[i][k] + dp[k][j])
Fill order: increasing interval length from 2 upward
lessons.explanation: Burst Balloons (#312) is a classic Hard DP problem. Bursting balloon i earns nums[i-1]*nums[i]*nums[i+1] coins, where left and right neighbors collapse when i is removed. This makes it hard to reason forward: bursting a balloon changes its neighbors. The key insight: think backward. Consider the LAST balloon to be burst in an interval (i,j) (where i and j are boundary sentinels). If k is the last balloon burst, then when k is burst, all other balloons between i and j are already gone, so k's neighbors are exactly nums[i] and nums[j]. This gives dp[i][j] = max over k of: nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] (coins from bursting k last) + dp[i][k] (coins from bursting everything in (i,k)) + dp[k][j] (coins from bursting everything in (k,j)). Extend nums with sentinel 1s at both ends. Fill the table by increasing interval length: small intervals before large ones. Final answer: dp[0][n+1] where n+1 is the right sentinel index.
lessons.analogy: Burst Balloons with last-balloon thinking is like demolishing buildings in a row. Instead of thinking about the order of demolitions (which changes the neighborhood dynamically), ask: which building is the last one to be demolished in each city block? The last building in a block is demolished when all others are gone, so its neighbors are the buildings at the block's boundaries. This fixed-neighbor property makes the problem tractable.

code_example.explanation: The fill order (increasing len) is critical: dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] must be computed before dp[i][j]. Since k is strictly between i and j, both dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] have smaller intervals (shorter len). Filling shorter intervals first guarantees all dependencies are available.

common_mistakes: Thinking of k as the FIRST balloon to burst instead of the LAST — if k is first, its neighbors change as others burst; if k is last, its neighbors are fixed (the boundary sentinels i and j); only the last-balloon framing gives a tractable recurrence
Forgetting to add sentinel 1s at both ends — without sentinels, the outermost balloons have undefined neighbors; sentinels handle the edge computation uniformly

Filling the DP table by row instead of by interval length — dp[i][j] depends on dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] where k is between i and j; filling by increasing interval length ensures all required subproblems are solved first

Sentinels are required because the DP table indices start at 1
Sentinels ensure the interval DP can compute all sub-intervals uniformly

logic_mcq.question: For `maxCoins([3,1,5,8])`, the extended array is [1,3,1,5,8,1]. The lesson traces dp[1][4]=135 for len=3 via k=3. Verify: what is the computation for k=3 in interval (1,4)?
options: k=3 in interval (1,4): coins=nums[1]*nums[3]*nums[4]=3*5*8=120; dp[1][3]=15 (max from bursting balloons strictly between 1 and 3); dp[3][4]=0 (no balloons strictly between 3 and 4); total=120+15+0=135; dp[1][4] takes max(64 from k=2, 135 from k=3)=135 — confirmed by the lesson's trace and direct execution
k=3: 3*5*8=120 with no sub-intervals
k=3 gives 64; k=2 gives 135; dp[1][4]=135
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: '(1,4): k=3: 3*5*8 + dp[1][3] + dp[3][4] = 120+15+0=135' — the formula is nums[left]*nums[k]*nums[right] + sub-interval costs; with left=1 (value 3), k=3 (value 5), right=4 (value 8): coins=3*5*8=120; plus dp[1][3]=15 (from the len=2 fill) and dp[3][4]=0 (adjacent, no balloon between); total=135.

logic_mcq.question: The fill order processes intervals by INCREASING LENGTH (len from 2 to n-1). Why must shorter intervals be computed BEFORE longer ones?
options: Longer intervals are independent of shorter ones; order doesn't matter

The transition `dp[i][j] = coins + dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]` depends on `dp[i][k]` (shorter sub-interval [i,k]) and `dp[k][j]` (shorter sub-interval [k,j]); for the recurrence to find valid cached values, both sub-intervals must already be computed; since every sub-interval (i,k) and (k,j) has length strictly less than (i,j), processing by increasing length guarantees all needed sub-results exist before they are needed
Shorter intervals are easier to compute; the order is for performance only
The len loop runs from large to small; shorter intervals are computed LAST
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Fill order: increasing interval length from 2 upward' — interval DP always fills by increasing size because the recurrence decomposes (i,j) into two strictly smaller intervals (i,k) and (k,j); bottom-up evaluation requires the smaller parts to be available before the larger part attempts to use them.

syntax_mcq.question: In `maxCoins`, the inner k-loop runs `for (let k = i+1; k < j; k++)`. Why is k STRICTLY BETWEEN i and j (k=i+1 to k<j), not including i or j?
options: i and j are sentinel positions and would cause array out of bounds

`dp[i][j]` represents coins from bursting balloons STRICTLY BETWEEN positions i and j — the sentinels/boundaries i and j are never burst in this sub-problem; k must be a real balloon in the interior (strictly between i and j); if k=i or k=j were allowed, we'd be 'bursting' the boundary positions which are not real balloons in this interval's context; the strict interior constraint is what makes the 'last balloon burst' insight work correctly
The strict bounds prevent computing dp[i][i+1] which is 0
k=i and k=j would create duplicate computations in the sum
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'dp[i][j] = max coins from bursting all balloons STRICTLY between i and j' — the interval boundaries i and j are fixed (they are either sentinels or the results of previous sub-problem boundaries); k must be chosen from the balloons actually in the interior; if k were allowed to equal i or j, we'd be treating the boundary as a balloon to burst, violating the interval DP's semantics.

core_patterns: 0/1 Knapsack 2D: dp[i][w]=max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wt]+val); use dp[i-1] not dp[i] on include branch
0/1 Knapsack 1D: same recurrence, RIGHT-TO-LEFT inner loop — prevents item reuse
Unbounded vs 0/1: only the loop direction differs (left-to-right vs right-to-left)
Three knapsack variants: MAX (max), COUNT (+=), BOOLEAN (||=) — same loop structure
Target Sum reduction: P=(sum+target)/2; count subsets summing to P (count variant knapsack)
Partition Equal Subset Sum: total even? then boolean knapsack to target=total/2
LIS O(n²): dp[i]=max LIS ending at i; answer=max(dp). Use strict < for strictly increasing.
LIS O(n log n): patience sort tails array; binary search leftmost ≥ x; length=LIS length
Edit Distance: match=diagonal (free), mismatch=1+min(diagonal,above,left); base dp[i][0]=i dp[0][j]=j
Interval DP (Burst Balloons): last-operation framing; fill by increasing gap length; O(n³)
